headline: Highly constructive on infrastructure debt, calling it the most attractive risk-adjusted opportunity in private credit
reasoning: Infrastructure credit benefits from hard asset collateral, low obsolescence, durable long-term contracts, and robust covenant structures that act as early-warning mechanisms. Historically, default rates have been below 1% through every cycle including 9/11, GFC, and COVID. Illiquidity premiums add to the return profile, and the market is structurally inefficient as investment banks continue to retrench from project and opportunistic financing due to capital constraints.
quote: We're very bullish on infrastructure debt due to the essential services, the essential assets that they're financing. The collateral is real, the contracts are durable, and we think the pricing is quite attractive.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Macquarie AM views current private credit stress as orderly and concentrated, not systemic — no GFC-style collapse anticipated
reasoning: Cherniak distinguishes the current environment from the GFC: stress is concentrated in specific sectors (leveraged software), structures (covenant-light), and vintages (2020–2022), rather than being systemic. Regulatory safeguards under the 1940 Act cap BDC leverage and require quarterly transparency at the asset level. The underlying loans continue to perform and multiple remediation tools (gates, secondary sales, co-investments) are available to managers.
quote: The word that I would use to describe what we're seeing or the view from a Macquarie asset management perspective around credit is orderly... we don't believe it's systemic.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Ancestry.com cited as example of durable software credit with near-infinite switching costs and no AI displacement risk
reasoning: Ancestry.com stores decades of genealogical DNA and family-tree data contributed by multiple generations of users; switching costs are effectively infinite. No AI startup can replicate 30 years of family history, making it structurally immune to the AI displacement risk threatening generic SaaS tools.
quote: Think about something like an Ancestry.com. It literally requires your DNA. Your family tree and its history is embedded in the software... The switching cost is almost infinite. And there's no AI startup that can replace 30 years of your family's genealogical history.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Macquarie AM sees 'great bifurcation' in private credit — stress in leveraged software vs. resilience in real assets
reasoning: Harlan Cherniak argues private credit is not monolithic and is entering a bifurcation phase: real and hard assets are holding up well, while leveraged software and parts of tech are showing visible cracks. The leveraged loan default rate is approaching 5.5% as of January, structures have loosened, and covenant-light loans originated 2020–2022 are now being stress tested. Infrastructure credit, by contrast, has historically maintained default rates below 1% through every cycle.
quote: This market is not monolithic. We believe that we're in the great bifurcation. Real asset and hard assets, those credits are holding up well. You're seeing some signs of stress in leverage software, as well as other pockets of technology, and those cracks are quite visible.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Macquarie research concludes AI investment boom is likely in early-to-mid innings, analogous to late 1997/early 1998 in the 1990s tech cycle
reasoning: Comparing current AI investment trajectories to the 1990s internet boom, McCormack's team found that tech investment has grown from single-digit to 30–35% of US non-residential investment. Indexing from the ChatGPT launch to the equivalent start of the 1993 tech boom suggests the cycle is currently at a 1997–1998 equivalent — with the prior boom running through end-2000. AI is assessed as more productivity-powerful than the internet, justifying investment even more than the prior cycle.
quote: If you look at growth rates, for example, it kind of looks like we're in late 1997, early 1998 in terms of tech spending... I think AI is probably more powerful than the internet and the technology revolution that happened back then.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: $4.6bn software take-private 'Sievert' cited as example of collateral value collapse — equity cushion cut in half
reasoning: The company was taken private at over 30x EV/EBITDA; current leverage sits at ~6.8x using 2027 estimates, which appears manageable, but peer comps (e.g. Adobe, Salesforce) have derated to ~9x EV/EBITDA. Terminal values have been revised down and the equity cushion underpinning the credit has compressed dramatically, effectively halving collateral values.
quote: One of those examples was a portfolio company called Sevent. It was a $4.6 billion take private over 30 times enterprise value to EBITDA... the peers that we tend to look at from a comparable company perspective and from an equity margin of safety standpoint are now trading down closer than nine times enterprise value to EBITDA.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Macquarie AM bullish on BDCs, characterising redemption headlines as a sentiment event rather than a systemic credit event
reasoning: There are over 165 BDCs with ~$500bn AUM and significant net inflows that have offset gross redemptions, a fact the media is largely ignoring. BDC structures include fund-level gates set at 5% quarterly — matching the natural 20% annual roll-off of five-year average loan tenors — and SEC-mandated quarterly asset-level disclosure. Leverage caps under the 1940 Act prevent systemic contagion. Cherniak views elevated redemptions as manageable and sees the BDC market as an opportunity.
quote: I'm not here to tell you that we don't expect those redemptions to increase... we're pretty bullish on the BDC opportunity set... over the last few quarters, you've seen significant net inflows that have offset some of those significant gross outflow figures, and they're only focused on the redemptions.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Software private credit facing 'yellow pages moment' as AI disruption and compressed collateral values create widespread stress
reasoning: Software represents 20–25% of the private credit market, with over half of credits rated B- or below and about $25 billion of loans trading below 80 cents on the dollar — nearly 30% of all distressed loans in the index. Original leverage attached at 5–6x debt/EBITDA underpinned by high EBITDA multiples (30x EV/EBITDA in some cases) is now exposed as peer comparables have compressed to ~9x and AI disruption threatens run-rate revenues. Generic, horizontally-deployed SaaS tools face the highest risk of AI displacement.
quote: Software may be having its yellow pages moment... there's about $25 billion of software loans that are trading below 80 cents on the dollar. It also represents almost 30% of all the distressed loans across the index.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Bullish on AI infrastructure credit as hyperscaler capex ($600–700bn in 2026 alone) drives massive demand for data centres, power, and fibre
reasoning: Hyperscaler capex commitments for 2026 aggregate close to $600–700bn (Amazon $200bn, Google $175bn), fuelling demand for data centres, GPUs, networking, and power infrastructure. Anthropic's ARR grew from $1bn to $19bn in 15 months — an unprecedented enterprise software growth rate — signalling the AI buildout is supply-constrained, not demand-constrained. This directly feeds infrastructure credit opportunities in power, data centres, and cooling.
quote: The cap commitment that had been out from some of the largest hyperscalers aggregates close to six, $700 billion for 2026 alone. Amazon at 200, Google at 175... this is just a great example of digital physical infrastructure at work.
episode_title: Private Credit at a crossroads?

headline: Regulated European utility networks — especially UK and Italian — are best insulated from energy price shock via inflation-linked revenues and asset bases
reasoning: Grid and network operators have regulated returns with inflation pass-through mechanisms, meaning revenues and regulated asset bases (RABs) automatically increase with inflation. UK and Italian frameworks are highlighted as particularly strong because both revenues and RABs are indexed to inflation, providing a high degree of investor protection. The main risk is political interference if the crisis is prolonged and governments act to shield consumers.
quote: UK and Italian regulated networks are best positioned. It's not only your revenues indexed to inflation, but also your rate base or your regulated asset base. There is a high degree of protection for investors in those assets.

headline: Airport volumes seen as resilient over the medium term as GDP — not fuel pricing — is the primary driver of air travel demand
reasoning: Oil constitutes roughly one-third of airline costs, meaning higher fuel prices feed directly into airfares, but historical analysis shows pricing is not a statistically significant driver of aggregate travel volumes — GDP growth is the overwhelming factor. Unless the oil shock is severe enough to materially dent GDP (e.g. oil at $150/bbl), airport throughput should hold up. Some short-term route-level disruption is expected.
quote: Really what we found was that at aggregated levels, the overwhelming driver was GDP growth. We ran a bunch of regressions and pricing was just not significant.

headline: Flexible gas infrastructure and battery storage assets are underpriced and should see value recognised as system flexibility becomes critical
reasoning: As the power system transitions to intermittent renewables, firm and flexible power capacity becomes essential insurance against weather-driven shocks. Gas infrastructure assets enabling flexibility have been underpriced for years, and the current crisis should prompt revaluation as well as policy debate about remuneration models — whether more regulated/decoupled or merchant. Macquarie is actively positioning into this theme.
quote: I think they've been underpriced for a number of years. Those assets or perhaps their inherent value will become a bit more recognised. This will kick off another round of debates, I suspect, as to how do electricity markets price, how do we remove or decouple gas prices from electricity prices.

headline: Oil price at current levels implies ~100-150bps headline inflation uplift and modest ~0.3-0.4pp GDP drag; $150/bbl scenario is far more disruptive
reasoning: If oil stays near current levels, headline inflation rises ~100-150bps with minimal core impact and GDP falls only ~0.3-0.4pp — a manageable shock. However, at $150/bbl, headline inflation could exceed 6-7% in developed markets, core could breach 4-4.5%, and GDP could be downgraded by 120bps, nearly wiping out European growth. The $150 scenario is seen as unlikely given political pressure on the US and Iran.
quote: If oil was to go to say $150 a barrel, which is being talked about... headline inflation will go north of 6%... and core rates will probably go north of four or four and a half percent. That's double central bank targets.

The combination of defensive equity characteristics with real return protection makes it attractive relative to bonds (rising yields) and expensive public credit (tight spreads).

headline: European merchant gas generators are insulated for 2025 via hedging but face margin risk from 2027 if crisis persists

headline: Port and shipping volumes expected to hold up well as shipping costs represent only 3-5% of end consumer prices
reasoning: Higher oil prices will push up shipping costs, but because shipping is only 3-5% of end consumer prices, the pass-through to end-demand is limited and volumes are unlikely to fall materially. headline: Government bonds likely to struggle if Middle East crisis continues given clear inflationary signal already embedded in rising yields
reasoning: Bond yields across the developed world have already risen in response to the crisis, reflecting market consensus that it is inflationary.
